newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia sees lower sugar returns this year.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia sees lower sugar returns this year.

text.p: Returns to sugar producers in the Australian state of Queensland were set to fall again in 1996/97, Queensland Sugar Corp (QSC) chief executive David Rutledge said in a statement.
This was because of lower world sugar prices, substantially lower regional premiums and the strengthening Australian dollar, he said.

Rutledge said world sugar prices had weakened by more than 30 percent over the past two years to their current 10.97 US cents a lb from 15.86 US cents a lb in January 1995 because of an oversupplied world sugar market.
As a consequence, 1996/97 pool returns were expected to be about 10 percent lower than 1995/96 returns of A$378.50 a tonne for No 1 pool and A$357.08 for No 2 pool sugar, he said.
However, record 1996 raw sugar production of 4.99 million tonnes meant that total payments to producers were expected to be down by only about two percent on 1995/96, he said.
Rutledge said analysts were forecasting a third successive year of surplus world sugar production.
World stocks as a percentage of consumption were now at levels comparable to those of the mid-1980s when sugar prices reached disastrously low levels, he said.

"However, while prices are not currently expected by analysts to reach these low levels again due to structural changes in the world market, QSC expects that returns to producers in 1997/98 could be reduced by a further five to 10 percent on anticipated 1996/97 pool returns," he said.
Rutledge said another factor which affected the corporation's sales revenue, and therefore pool returns, was the premium it received for sales in the Asian region.

Recent good crops and low demand in the Asian region had increased the availability of raw sugar, with the regional premium falling to less than 0.5 US cents a lb from 1.5 US cents a lb in September 1996, he said.
A major third factor affecting this year's pool returns was the appreciation of the Australian dollar in 1996/97, he said.

During the crushing season, the Australian dollar was at historically high levels which coincided with the period in which the corporation receives most of its foreign currency income from sugar sales, he said.

The corporation's financial risk management programme had to some extent reduced the impact on the industry of lower prices and the fluctuating dollar through the use of forward selling and hedging activities, he said.
Australia's sugar crush runs from June to December.
